text: Continual improvement practice. The last of the three practices in this chapter, and the one that ties back to something you already learned.

ITIL 4's purpose statement: align the organization's practices and services with changing business needs, through the ongoing identification and improvement of services, components, practices, or any element involved in managing products and services. The key word is 'ongoing.' This isn't a project with a start and end date -- it's a standing capability, the organization's ability to keep noticing where things could be better and actually doing something about it, indefinitely.

ITIL 4 gives this a repeatable structure: the Continual Improvement Model, seven steps in order. What is the vision -- understand the objective. Where are we now -- assess honestly, with real data. Where do we want to be -- define measurable targets. How do we get there -- plan it. Take action. Did we get there -- evaluate against the targets. And how do we keep the momentum going -- which loops right back into step one for whatever comes next.

A common misreading is picturing a dedicated 'continual improvement team' running this quietly in the background. ITIL 4 says that's the wrong model. It's meant to be embedded in everyone's daily work -- a service desk agent noticing a recurring question and suggesting a knowledge article, a change advisory board member spotting that one change type keeps causing the same minor incident, a problem manager noticing a pattern across three unrelated-looking tickets. No special title required.

This connects directly back to Chapter 3. The Service Value Chain's 'Improve' activity exists to keep every other activity getting better over time. The continual improvement practice is how that actually happens, day to day -- from a single service desk script up to an organization-wide process.

That closes out Chapters 4 through 6 -- ten core ITIL 4 practices, each with a narrow purpose, each feeding information to a neighbor. Next, Chapter 7 turns from framework theory to a real platform: how a tool like ServiceNow actually implements the practices you've just learned.
